The Deputy Superintendent General of Indian Affairs, Ottawa.


DEPARTMENT OF INDIAN AFFAIRS, October 29, 1924.

DEAR SIR, - I have your letter of the 27th instant with reference to an advance made to Matt Bernard of his salary as
Truant Officer and Caretaker of the Golden Lake school for the last fiscal year.

Mr. Bernard is Chief of the Band, and has been for several years acting in the capacity of Truant Officer and Caretaker
for the school. Having confidence in his reliability the Department made the advance in question to enable him to carry
out some building operations in connection with a lot which he had acquired on the reserve. Had this not been done
the Department might have been under obligation to make a loan to the Chief.

The services, covered by this payment have been fully and satisfactorily rendered.

<!-- page 572 -->
Yours very truly,
D.C. SCOTT, D.S.G.


The Assistant Auditor General.

<!-- page 573 -->
AUDITOR GENERAL'S OFFICE, November 17, 1924.

SIR, - I beg to acknowledge receipt of your letter of the 29th ulto., stating the circumstances under which payment was
made in advance to Matt Bernard of his salary for the year 1923 - 24 as Truant Officer and Caretaker of the Golden
Lake Indian School.

I am of the opinion that the circumstances mentioned were not sufficient to warrant the payment of salary for a whole
year in advance, even although the salary was small. In fact I consider that under no circumstances whatever should a
salary or any part of a salary be paid in advance, with the exception of the Civil Government Salaries at Ottawa,
which, under special authority are paid at the middle of the month.


I am, Sir, your obedient servant,
WM. KEARNS, Asst. A.G.


The Deputy Superintendent General of Indian Affairs, Ottawa.

Vote 279, Indian Education: Payment of Overdraft by Six Nations School Board


AUDITOR GENERAL'S OFFICE, October 28, 1924.

SIR, - Cheque No. 1043 drawn against the vote for Indian Education, 1923 - 24, is for the payment of $920.86 to the
Bank of Montreal in settlement of an overdraft of the Six Nations School Board account for the fiscal year ended
March 31st, 1923. Cheque No. 6435, also in favour of the Bank of Montreal, is for the payment of an overdraft of
$220.65 at the close of the fiscal year 1923 - 24.

Kindly inform me if any examinations were made by an officer of your department of the accounts of the Six Nations
School Board before these overdrafts were paid by you. If any such examinations were made I should like to be
furnished with a copy of any reports which may have been made by the examining officer.

I should also like to be informed as to any special reason there may have been for paying these overdrafts, from your
vote for Indian Education. The Six Nations Schools are, I understand, administered by a School Board who receive an
annual grant of $9,000 from the Band Funds, towards which the Department contributes $2,500. In addition to that
grant various expenses connected with the schools are also paid from the Band Funds. The amounts at the credit of the
Six Nations Indian account at the close of the fiscal year 1922 - 23 and 1923 - 24 were as follows: -

March 31, 1923, capital, $678,782.10; interest, $10,937.65.

March 31, 1924, capital, $676,508.43; interest, $23,323.46.

From which there would appear to have been ample funds at the close of each fiscal year to meet the comparatively
small overdrafts.


I am, Sir, your obedient servant,
WM. KEARNS, Asst. A.G.


The Deputy Superintendent General of Indian Affairs, Ottawa.


DEPARTMENT OF INDIAN AFFAIRS, November 7, 1924.

<!-- page 574 -->
SIR, - I have your letter of the 28th ultimo, with reference to the Department's contribution from Parliamentary
Appropriation for Indian Education to the current expenses at the Six Nations Indian Schools. In reply I wish

<!-- page 575 -->
to inform you that it is considered advisable to use only $6,500 from Band Funds for the day schools on this reserve.
In the past, the payment from Appropriation was $2,500 which made a total of $9,000, which was all that was
required. Of late years, the expenses have increased and approximately $10,200 is necessary for the conduct of the
eleven schools. The school board accounts are examined and passed upon by the Superintendent of the Six Nations
Reserve.


Yours very truly,
D.C. SCOTT, D.S.G.


The Assistant Auditor General.


AUDITOR GENERAL'S OFFICE, November 17, 1924.

SIR, - I am in receipt of your letter of the 7th inst., in reply to mine of the 28th ulto., with reference to the payment of
two overdrafts in the Bank of Montreal on the Six Nations School Board account, and note your statement that the
school board accounts are examined and passed upon by the Superintendent of the Six Nations. Reserve.

As the payments in question are for definite amounts arrived at by an examination of the accounts made by the
Superintendent of the band, I am of opinion that a statement of those accounts should be submitted to this office in
order that the amounts of the payments may be verified.


I am, sir, your obedient servant,
WM. KEARNS, Asst. A.G.


The Deputy Superintendent General of Indian Affairs, Ottawa.

Vote 279, Indian Education: Coal purchased for Bersimis Day School


AUDITOR GENERAL'S OFFICE, November 5, 1924.

SIR, - Education cheque No. 2755 of 1923 - 24 is for the payment of $228 to Louis Verreault & Son, of Petits Mechins
for 10 tons of coal, in sacks, for the Bersimis Day School. Cheque No. 4416 of the same year is for a payment of
$524.32 to Madden & Son of Quebec for 26.09 tons coal in sacks, also for the Bersimis Day School.

So far as I can gather from the accounts received at this office the Bersimis school was closed during the fall and
winter of 1923 - 24, a new combined boarding and day school being in process of erection, which was completed
about the beginning of February, 1924.

I should like to be informed whether this coal, or any part of it, was used for heating the new building while it was in
the contractor's hands, or if it was purchased before the close of navigation for the sole purpose of heating the building
after it was taken over from the contractor.

The cost of the coal includes 547 sacks at 10 cents and 126 at 15 cents, amounting to $72.70. Kindly let me know if
these sacks were returnable on repayment, or if not what disposition was made of them.


I am, sir, your obedient servant,

<!-- page 576 -->
WM. KEARNS, Asst. A.G.


The Deputy Superintendent General of Indian Affairs, Ottawa.
